ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Gauging | Memphis, TN
ut.description: On-site ultrasonic testing in Memphis, TN: wall thickness surveys, corrosion checks and shear-wave weld examination for terminals and plants. Get a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Gauging in Memphis, Tennessee
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II ultrasonic technicians to Memphis, Tennessee for wall thickness surveys, corrosion monitoring and shear-wave examination of welds. The work typically covers river terminal tanks and piping on President's Island, plant process lines, structural steel and fabricated vessels across the Mid-South. Send us the asset list, the governing code and the access conditions, and we will scope the job around it. Request a UT quote for your Memphis site.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Memphis

Memphis sits on the Mississippi River, and the Port of Memphis describes a stretch of about fifteen river miles with dozens of waterfront facilities, most of them concentrated on President's Island. The terminals there handle bulk liquids such as petroleum, along with cement, steel, fertilizer and grain. That mix creates a steady need for thickness data: atmospheric storage tanks, transfer piping, loading arms, dock piping and the supports that carry them all lose wall to corrosion under insulation, soil-side attack and splash-zone wetting.

Beyond the river, the city is a rail and highway crossroads, and the region supports food and chemical processing, metal fabrication, power generation and distribution warehousing. Each of those has a different UT question. A fertilizer or chemical line asks how much wall remains at an elbow. A fabrication shop asks whether a groove weld on a crane runway beam has lack of fusion. A warehouse operator asks whether a heavy base plate weld on racking or a dock leveler frame has cracked. The ultrasonic method answers all three, provided the technician matches the technique to the question.

Memphis also lives with large Mississippi crossings and the steel highway structures that feed them. Owners and engineers of that kind of steel use UT mainly to examine welded repair details and to confirm plate thickness where section loss is suspected, working under the owner's bridge or structural code rather than a generic procedure.

What UT finds in Memphis assets, and what it does not

Ultrasonic testing sends sound into the material and listens for what returns. For thickness, the time between the front-surface pulse and the back-wall echo, multiplied by the sound velocity of the material, gives wall thickness. For welds, an angled shear wave travels through the weld volume and reflects from planar flaws such as lack of fusion, incomplete penetration and cracks.

On Memphis carbon steel tanks and pipe, the method is very good at general wall loss and localized pitting, provided the surface is cleaned enough for coupling. It is less reliable where the outer surface is heavily scaled, where the coating is thick and soft, or where the inside surface is so rough that the back-wall echo scatters. Cast iron and coarse-grained cast or centrifugally cast pipe attenuate sound strongly, so readings may be noisy or absent. Austenitic stainless welds also scatter shear waves, and a technique that works on carbon steel may need a different probe and a trial on a mock-up.

UT is not a surface-crack method. A tight surface-breaking crack at a toe may be easier to find with magnetic particle inspection in Memphis on ferromagnetic steel or liquid penetrant testing in Memphis on non-magnetic alloys. A good job plan names which method answers which question.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Memphis UT work

The governing document for a UT job is the construction or in-service code the owner already works under. For fabricated pressure equipment, ASME Section V sets the examination method: Article 4 covers ultrasonic examination of welds, Article 5 covers ultrasonic examination of materials, and Article 23 carries SE-797 for contact pulse-echo thickness measurement. Acceptance is then taken from the code of construction, for example ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 for vessel welds or Table 341.3.2 of ASME B31.3 for process piping. Structural steel follows AWS D1.1, which includes ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and bridge steel follows AWS D1.5.

In-service equipment is a different regime. API 510, API 570 and API 653 place responsibility for the inspection plan with the owner's authorized inspector. Atlantis does not act as that inspector. We perform the ultrasonic work, report the thickness at each condition monitoring location, and give your inspector the data to calculate corrosion rate and remaining life.

Tennessee requires periodic state inspection of boilers and of unfired pressure vessels above stated size and pressure limits, administered through the Workplace Regulations and Compliance division of the state labor department. Repairs and alterations to that equipment follow the National Board Inspection Code. If a UT finding on a Memphis vessel leads to a repair, the repair plan and its examination requirements come through the owner's chosen inspection channel, not through us.

Where process safety management applies, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) expects inspection and testing in line with recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and thickness records are one of the most common pieces of evidence for it.

How a UT job is done

A thickness survey begins with a grid or a list of condition monitoring locations marked on the equipment. The technician prepares each spot, removes loose scale, applies couplant and calibrates the instrument on a step block of the same material, covering the expected thickness range. A dual-element probe is the usual choice on corroded steel because it handles rough and pitted surfaces better than a single-element probe, and an A-scan display lets the technician see the waveform and avoid doubled or false readings on thin or laminated wall. Hot lines call for high-temperature probes and couplant, with the temperature recorded so a correction can be applied.

Weld examination is a different technique. The technician builds a reference level or distance-amplitude curve from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, selects an angle beam (commonly forty-five, sixty or seventy degrees depending on thickness and weld geometry), and scans from both sides of the weld where access allows. Indications are located, sized against the reference level and evaluated against the acceptance table the code names. Every setup is recorded so another Level II can repeat it. Our ultrasonic testing service page describes the general technique in more detail, and the ultrasonic testing guide covers the physics.

Who performs the work

Technicians who mobilize to Memphis are qualified under Atlantis's written practice, written to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up the instrument, calibrates, performs the examination and interprets the results against the procedure. An ASNT Level III approves the procedures and reviews the reports. Our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis has no office in Memphis: technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, which keeps the crew matched to the job rather than to a fixed roster.

If you need a procedure written for a specific code, or want your own written practice reviewed, see our Level III consulting and written practice development pages.

What a Memphis UT report contains

  • Component or line number, location and a sketch or isometric reference.
  • Procedure number and revision, and the code section it follows.
  • Instrument, probe, calibration block, couplant and the calibration check records.
  • Technician name and qualification level.
  • For thickness: a reading at each location, nominal thickness, minimum required thickness where the owner supplies it, and a thickness grid for area surveys.
  • For welds: scan plan, reference level, indication location and length, amplitude, and accept or reject against the named criteria.

The report is written so an owner's inspector, an insurer or an auditor can follow it without a phone call.

Planning a UT job in Memphis

Memphis summers are hot and humid, and steel surfaces in the sun can be hot enough to damage standard couplant and probes. Cold snaps are shorter than in the upper Midwest but do occur, and ice on river terminal ramps changes how access is planned. Humidity also keeps surfaces damp, so surface preparation and drying matter for couplant behavior. Dock and terminal work follows the facility's own access and safety rules, and plants usually require site orientation and badging before work starts, so give us those requirements when you request a quote.

Outage windows matter too. Many process facilities schedule thickness work at turnaround so the equipment is cold, empty and scaffolded, and requests tend to cluster in spring and fall. River levels can affect terminal operations, so we plan around the facility's own operating schedule.

Typical problems a Memphis UT survey is asked to settle

The questions that bring owners to ultrasonic testing along the Mississippi corridor are fairly consistent. A tank owner wants to know whether the shell course nearest the bottom has thinned since the last survey, and whether the annular plate under it is still sound. A pipeline or terminal operator wants thickness at elbows, reducers and dead legs where flow turbulence or stagnant water speeds up corrosion. A fabricator wants evidence that a thick-section groove weld was fused through before it is painted and shipped. An insurer or lender wants a baseline before equipment changes hands.

Each of these calls for a slightly different plan. A bottom-adjacent shell survey needs a tight vertical grid and a decision about how to treat coating. A dead-leg survey needs a wide sweep of the pipe circumference, because the thinnest wall is often at the six o'clock position where water collects. A thick-section weld may need a lower frequency to penetrate and a trial on a calibration block that reflects the actual joint geometry. Agreeing the plan with your engineer before mobilization saves repeat visits, and it also makes the resulting numbers directly comparable to the previous survey.

Records matter as much as readings. If last year's survey used a grid of one hundred locations and this year's uses a different layout, no one can say with confidence whether a thin spot is new. We therefore mark locations, photograph them where permitted, and keep the grid identical to the one on your drawings so that trends can be read directly from the data.

UT, MT or PT for your Memphis job

Use UT when the question is about wall thickness or the inside of a weld. Use MT when the question is surface cracking in carbon or low-alloy steel, and PT when the surface is non-magnetic or the item is non-ferrous. Most real jobs combine two of them: for example thickness gauging at CMLs plus MT at repair welds.

Training your own UT technicians

If you would rather build in-house capability, we offer UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 training, and the UT simulator lets trainees practice scanning before they touch real equipment. Under SNT-TC-1A your company, not the course provider, certifies its own personnel, so see the NDT training for Memphis page for how that works for employers.

faq.q: Can Atlantis do ultrasonic thickness testing on storage tanks in Memphis?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to the terminal or plant and take readings at the condition monitoring locations you specify, then report them to your authorized inspector, who calculates corrosion rate and remaining life.

faq.q: Do you perform ultrasonic weld inspection in Memphis?
faq.a: Yes. Shear-wave examination of groove welds is done with angle beams against a reference level, and acceptance is taken from the construction code the weld was built under, such as ASME or AWS D1.1.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Memphis?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, so the crew is matched to the job. You give us the location, access rules and codes, and we plan the visit around them.

faq.q: Will Atlantis act as the API 510, 570 or 653 inspector on a Tennessee vessel or tank?
faq.a: No. Your owner-user authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection program. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic work and delivers the thickness data and reports your inspector needs.

faq.q: What surface temperature limits apply to UT thickness readings?
faq.a: Standard probes and couplants have limits, so hot lines need high-temperature probes and couplant, and the surface temperature is recorded so a velocity correction can be applied. Tell us the operating temperature when you request a quote.

faq.q: What does UT miss that I should worry about?
faq.a: UT can miss tight surface-breaking cracks, struggles on heavily scaled or very rough surfaces, and is difficult on cast iron and coarse-grained material. For surface cracks we pair it with magnetic particle or liquid penetrant testing.

faq.q: What should I send to get a UT quote for a Memphis job?
faq.a: Send the asset list or drawings, materials, nominal thickness, operating temperature, the governing code, and site access and badging requirements. A short call or email lets us confirm scope and the qualifications you need.

faq.q: Which codes govern ultrasonic examination on Memphis projects?
faq.a: ASME Section V Articles 4, 5 and 23 set the method, while acceptance comes from the construction code, such as ASME Section VIII, ASME B31.3 or AWS D1.1. Your contract names the edition.

faq.q: Can you train our own staff in ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Yes. We offer UT Level 1 and Level 2 training with a practice simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A your company certifies its own people against its written practice, and we can help you build that practice.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Memphis, TN | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Memphis, TN: weld, crane, rail-car and steel structure crack checks with yokes and wet or dry particles. Request a MT quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Memphis, Tennessee
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II technicians to Memphis, Tennessee to perform magnetic particle inspection (MPI, also called mag particle testing) on welds, castings, forgings and structural steel. Typical work includes weld toes on fabricated steel, lifting equipment at river and rail yards, and repair welds on plant equipment. Tell us the part, the material and the code, and we will plan the examination. Request an MT quote for your Memphis site.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Memphis

Few American cities handle as much heavy freight as Memphis. The Mississippi River port, a dense rail network, interstate highways and a large air cargo operation all move steel equipment, and all of that equipment is subject to cracking from fatigue and overload. The Port of Memphis lists dozens of waterfront facilities, with President's Island carrying most of them, and the terminals there handle steel, cement, fertilizer, grain and petroleum products. Cranes, hoppers, conveyor frames, barge-loading structures and the pads and padeyes that lift them are all carbon steel and all candidates for MT.

Inland, fabrication shops and metal processors weld structural steel, tanks, trailers and machinery frames. Rail yards and shops deal with couplers, truck frames and welded repairs. Warehouses and distribution centers use heavy racking, lift trucks and dock equipment, where a cracked weld can drop a load. Power and process plants add pressure-equipment attachment welds, support lugs, nozzle welds and the repair welds that follow maintenance outages.

The common thread is carbon or low-alloy steel with surface-breaking cracks at weld toes, fillet roots and sharp changes of section. This is the situation magnetic particle testing is built for.

What MT finds, and where it stops

MT works only on ferromagnetic material. When the part is magnetized, a crack that breaks the surface or lies just beneath it interrupts the magnetic field and pulls fine iron particles into a visible line. The method is fast and sensitive for tight cracks, laps, seams and lack of sidewall fusion at the surface, and it works through thin non-magnetic coatings if the procedure allows.

It does not work on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper or most nickel alloys, because those are not ferromagnetic. It also loses sensitivity with depth: a flaw more than a short distance below the surface will not produce an indication. And the field must cross the discontinuity at a favorable angle. A crack running parallel to the field lines can pass unnoticed, which is why the code requires examination in two directions roughly at right angles.

For non-magnetic Memphis assets such as stainless piping or aluminum structures, liquid penetrant testing in Memphis is the surface method of choice. For wall loss or internal weld defects, see ultrasonic testing in Memphis.

Codes and acceptance criteria

Magnetic particle examination is controlled by ASME Section V Article 7 when the job is under ASME construction or repair rules. The Article sets lifting-power requirements for yokes, particle and illumination requirements, the two-direction rule, and when demagnetization is required. Acceptance comes from the governing code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel and AWS D1.5 for bridge steel. ASTM E709 is the general guide and ASTM E1444 the practice that many specifications reference.

Tennessee's boiler and pressure vessel program, run through the Workplace Regulations and Compliance division of the state labor department, inspects boilers and larger unfired pressure vessels, and repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code. When an MT examination is part of a repair, the examination requirements are written into the repair plan that your owner-user inspector or authorized inspection agency accepts. Atlantis performs and reports the examination; it does not take over the owner's inspection responsibilities under API 510, API 570 or API 653.

How an MT examination is done

Surface preparation comes first. Paint, scale, weld spatter and oil must be removed enough for particles to move and for the part to be magnetized properly. Weld surfaces may need light grinding if the profile masks indications.

For field work the portable electromagnetic yoke is the main tool. An AC yoke is checked for a lifting power of at least ten pounds at the maximum pole spacing used, while a DC or permanent-magnet yoke must lift at least forty pounds. The yoke is placed across the weld, particles are applied while the field is on, and the area is examined for indications. The yoke is then rotated roughly ninety degrees and the examination repeated, so that cracks in any direction are caught. Prods are an alternative on thick sections or in shops where arcing is controlled. Dry powder suits rough or hot surfaces, and wet visible particles suit smoother surfaces. Wet fluorescent particles give the highest sensitivity, viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, and they are common in shop work on critical parts.

Indications are classified as relevant or non-relevant, measured, and compared with the acceptance table. Disputed indications can be wiped clean and re-examined, and when a part will be welded, machined or put into rotating service, demagnetization removes residual fields that could interfere. Our magnetic particle testing page and the MT complete guide explain the technique further, and the Article 7 explainer walks through the code requirements.

Who does the work

MT in Memphis is performed by technicians qualified under Atlantis's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up the equipment, performs the examination, interprets and records the results. An ASNT Level III approves the written procedure and reviews the report. The company is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis has no office in Memphis, so technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope.

If your fabrication or maintenance team needs its own MT procedure to a specific code, our Level III consulting can write and qualify it.

What the MT report shows

  • Part or weld identification, location and drawing reference.
  • Procedure number and revision and the code it implements.
  • Equipment: yoke type, measured lifting power, particle type and lot, and the light meter for visible or UV-A examination.
  • Surface condition, technique and the two examination directions.
  • Every indication with location and size, and accept or reject against the named table.
  • Technician name and qualification level, with the date and results of any re-examination or demagnetization check.

Planning an MT job in Memphis

Heat and humidity are the main practical issues. In summer, steel left in the sun can be too hot for wet particles, which dry out and lose mobility, so the procedure must be qualified for the surface temperature or the work shifted to cooler hours. Wet particle carriers also behave differently in humid air, and rain delays are common on open terminals. In winter, moisture can freeze on shaded steel, and the particle suspension must be kept above its limit.

Most Memphis facilities require badging and safety orientation, and river terminals have their own access control. If fluorescent examination is planned, we need a space that can be darkened, or a portable enclosure, and we agree the lighting arrangement before arrival. Outage seasons in spring and fall bring peak demand, so early scheduling helps.

Typical crack sites on Memphis steel

Knowing where cracks start makes an MT job faster and the report more useful. On welded crane runway beams and gantry legs at river and rail yards, fatigue cracks tend to begin at the toes of attachment welds, at the ends of stiffeners and at cope holes, where stress concentrates under repeated load cycles. On barge-loading structures and hopper frames, cracks often begin where a gusset meets a flange or at the weld that joins a lifting lug to the structure, because lifting loads are applied there repeatedly. On trailers and truck frames, fatigue cracks follow the welds that attach cross members and spring hangers, and they grow from the weld toe into the parent plate.

In plant service the pattern changes. Pressure equipment attachment welds, such as support lugs and saddle welds, crack from thermal cycling and restrained expansion. Repair welds are examined because a repair is the area most likely to contain lack of fusion or cracking in the heat-affected zone, particularly on thick or higher-carbon material that was welded without adequate preheat. When we plan the examination, we ask for the original weld map or the repair plan so we can check these areas first and spend the most time where cracks are most likely to form.

Choosing wet or dry particles and visible or fluorescent light

The right particle system depends on the surface, the temperature and the sensitivity the code expects. Dry powder is used on rough as-welded surfaces and on warm steel, where wet carriers would evaporate, and it is sensitive to subsurface indications when used with AC. Wet visible particles in aerosol cans are practical on cleaner machined or ground surfaces and give better sensitivity to fine surface cracks. Wet fluorescent particles are the most sensitive option and are preferred for critical parts, but they need the darkened area and UV-A lamp already described, and the lamp intensity and ambient white light must be measured and recorded.

Contrast paint, a thin white background coat, is often applied to dark or rough steel before visible wet particles to improve the visibility of indications. Particle concentration for wet suspensions must be checked with a settling test at the start of work and whenever the bath looks weak. These checks add minutes to a job, but they are what separates a defensible examination from one that is questioned months later in an audit.

MT, PT or UT for your Memphis job

Choose MT for surface cracking on carbon steel, PT where the metal is not ferromagnetic, and UT where the question is wall thickness or an internal weld flaw. Often the job needs two methods, such as MT on a repair weld after UT shows thinning. Use the three pages for Memphis together when planning scope.

Training your own MT technicians

Plant and shop owners who want their own people qualified can take MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 with us. The employer remains the certifying body under SNT-TC-1A, and the Memphis NDT training page explains how courses connect to your own written practice. The practice tests are a useful self-check before an exam.

faq.q: Can you perform magnetic particle inspection on welds in Memphis?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your shop or plant, examine welds with an AC or DC yoke in two directions, and report indications against the acceptance criteria of the governing code such as ASME or AWS D1.1.

faq.q: Does magnetic particle testing work on stainless steel?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel is not ferromagnetic, so MT will not work on it. For stainless piping or aluminum structures in Memphis, liquid penetrant testing is the surface method we use instead.

faq.q: How deep can magnetic particle inspection detect a crack?
faq.a: MT is a surface method that finds discontinuities open to the surface and a short distance below it. Deeper flaws do not form indications, so volumetric concerns call for ultrasonic testing.

faq.q: Can MT be done on hot surfaces in Memphis summers?
faq.a: Wet particles lose mobility on hot steel, so the procedure must be qualified for the temperature or the work scheduled for cooler periods. Dry powder is sometimes better on rough, warm surfaces.

faq.q: Do you provide fluorescent magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Yes, when a darkened area is available. Fluorescent particles are examined under UV-A light and give the highest sensitivity, so we agree the lighting arrangement and area before mobilizing.

faq.q: Is demagnetization part of the service?
faq.a: When residual magnetism could interfere with welding, machining, instruments or rotating service, demagnetization is included in the procedure, and the residual field is checked and recorded in the report.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a Memphis office or crew?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Memphis. Qualified technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, so we need site address, access requirements and your preferred code reference at quote stage.

faq.q: Which standards cover magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 7 covers the method for code work, with acceptance in ASME Section VIII, B31.3, AWS D1.1 or D1.5 depending on the asset. ASTM E709 and E1444 are widely referenced.

faq.q: How do I get my own people qualified in MT?
faq.a: Our MT Level 1 and Level 2 courses cover theory and practical skills. Your company certifies its own personnel under its written practice, and we can help you draft or review that practice.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Memphis, TN | LPT
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Memphis, TN: dye penetrant checks of welds on stainless, aluminum and carbon steel at plants and shops. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Memphis, Tennessee
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Memphis, Tennessee for liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection or PT. The method reveals cracks, laps and porosity that are open to the surface of non-porous metals, which makes it the standard tool for stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic alloys. Send us the material, surface condition and code, and we will plan the examination. Request a PT quote for your Memphis site.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Memphis

Memphis has a mixed industrial base, and much of it uses metals that magnetic particle testing cannot examine. Food, beverage and chemical processors along the Mississippi corridor rely on stainless steel piping, tanks and heat exchangers, where weld cracking or crevice attack must be found before a leak contaminates product. Fertilizer and chemical terminals near the river use stainless and nickel alloy components in corrosive service. Fabrication shops weld aluminum trailers, tank bodies and structural frames. Machine shops and repair facilities check castings, valves and welded repairs on non-ferrous parts.

Logistics also creates PT work. Aircraft ground equipment, aluminum cargo containers and handling gear take heavy daily use, and stress cracks start at welds and fasteners. Penetrant testing is portable, requires no electricity in its simplest form, and can be applied at a hangar, a dock or a workshop bench.

For carbon steel pipe and structural welds in the same city, magnetic particle inspection in Memphis is usually the faster surface method. PT can also be used on carbon steel when MT is impractical or when the code calls for penetrant.

What PT finds, and what it misses

Penetrant testing works by capillary action. A liquid with very low surface tension is applied to a clean surface and given time to enter any crack open to the surface. After excess penetrant is removed, a developer draws liquid back out and makes the indication visible as colored or fluorescent lines and dots. It detects only discontinuities that are open to the surface, so a crack hidden under smeared metal, a weld overlay, a plating layer or a heavy paint film will not show.

It does not work on porous materials, because the penetrant soaks into the surface and creates background that hides everything. It is also highly sensitive to cleanliness: oil, rust, scale and even the smear from grinding or wire brushing can close crack mouths. That is why surface preparation and pre-cleaning are treated as part of the method, not as a courtesy. PT also gives no information about depth. When wall loss or internal weld quality is the question, ultrasonic testing in Memphis is the right tool.

Codes and acceptance criteria

For ASME-controlled work, ASME Section V Article 6 defines how penetrant examination is carried out, including materials, dwell, removal, developer application and evaluation. Acceptance then comes from the construction code: Appendix 8 of ASME Section VIII Division 1, paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 of ASME B31.3, ASME B31.1 for power piping, AWS D1.1 for structural welds, and AWS D1.6 for stainless structural steel. ASTM E165 is the general industry practice commonly cited when the contract does not point to Section V.

One detail trips up many first-time buyers: the standard method covers a limited temperature band for both the part and the penetrant materials, and outside that band the procedure must be demonstrated at the actual temperature. On Memphis jobs that matters in July and August, when stainless surfaces in the sun can run far above the range, and during the occasional hard freeze. Another is the control of contaminants: when examining nickel alloys, stainless steel or titanium, the code requires penetrant materials with limits on sulfur, chlorine and fluorine, because these elements can attack the metal. We confirm material lots and certifications before we start.

Tennessee's boiler and pressure vessel rules apply state inspection to boilers and larger unfired vessels, and repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code. If a PT finding leads to repair, the repair plan runs through the owner's chosen inspection route. Atlantis supplies the examination and the report; it does not act as an API 510, 570 or 653 inspector.

How a PT job is done

The procedure follows a fixed sequence. The surface is cleaned with solvent or mechanical methods, and any mechanical cleaning that could smear metal is followed by etching if the procedure requires it. The surface is then dried completely. Penetrant is applied by spray, brush or immersion and left to dwell for the time the procedure specifies, which depends on material, flaw type and temperature. Excess penetrant is removed according to the method: water washable, post-emulsifiable or solvent removable. Developer is then applied in a thin, even coat, and the part is examined after the developing time.

Visible dye penetrant, usually red against a white developer, suits field work in daylight. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive and is examined under UV-A light in a darkened area, which is common for critical shop work. Solvent-removable penetrant is the most common field choice because it needs no water supply or drain. Indications are recorded with location, size and orientation, evaluated against the acceptance table, and the part is post-cleaned afterward to remove residue, which is particularly important on stainless steel that will go back into service. Our penetrant testing page and the Article 6 explainer give more technique detail, and the MT versus PT comparison helps choose between them.

Who does the work

Memphis PT is done by technicians qualified under Atlantis's written practice, which is written to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs the examination, interprets indications and records results. An ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Penetrant procedures for Memphis work are reviewed at the top level by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis has no office in Memphis; technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope.

If your plant needs an approved penetrant procedure that fits its own equipment and codes, our Level III consulting team can write and review it.

What the PT report shows

  • Component, weld or area identification and a reference to the drawing.
  • Material and surface condition, plus the cleaning method used before and after.
  • Penetrant system: type, method, manufacturer, product family and lot numbers, with contaminant certifications where required.
  • Surface and ambient temperature at the time of examination, dwell and developing times.
  • Every indication with location, size and orientation, with accept or reject against the named criteria.
  • Technician name and qualification level, and the procedure revision.

Planning a PT job in Memphis

Heat and humidity dominate planning. Hot surfaces make penetrant evaporate before it can enter cracks, and the developer can dry too quickly. We therefore check surface temperature at the start of each shift and schedule examination for cooler hours or shaded surfaces when necessary. On damp days, drying the part completely before penetrant is applied takes more time than on dry days. Winter jobs on river terminals face the opposite problem: cold steel slows penetrant action, and a procedure qualified at the lower temperature may be required.

Access to plants and terminals requires badging and orientation, and food and beverage plants have additional hygiene rules for tools and materials. Tell us about chemical restrictions at the quote stage. Some facilities prohibit certain solvents or require water-based materials near product areas, and we can specify penetrant systems to match.

Choosing the penetrant system for a Memphis job

The penetrant family is chosen from three variables: the surface, the environment and the sensitivity the code expects. Type I fluorescent penetrants are examined under UV-A light and are the most sensitive, which is why they are used on machined parts, critical welds and aerospace-style components. Type II visible penetrants are viewed in white light and are the usual field choice. Within each type, Method A is water washable, Method B is post-emulsifiable and Method C is solvent removable. Water washable systems are fast on rough surfaces but can over-wash shallow cracks. Solvent removable systems are slower but are controlled by hand and dominate field work at plants and terminals in the Memphis area.

Sensitivity levels also matter. Low sensitivity penetrants suit coarse surfaces and larger defects, while high sensitivity penetrants are used where fine cracks are the concern, such as fatigue cracking on stainless or aluminum parts. The procedure names the system and the acceptable alternatives, and every can used is recorded by lot number. Mixing products from different manufacturers is not permitted, because the cleaner, penetrant and developer are designed as a family and mixing them can reduce sensitivity or cause reactions.

Common surface-preparation mistakes

Most poor penetrant results can be traced to preparation rather than to the penetrant itself. Grit blasting or wire brushing peens the surface and can close the mouths of fine cracks, so penetrant cannot enter them. Paint remnants and oxide films block the opening. Oil and grease inside cracks keep the penetrant out, and residual cleaning solvents inside cracks can dilute the penetrant or evaporate too slowly. On welds, spatter and slag must be cleaned from the surface and the adjacent base metal so that the whole heat-affected zone is exposed.

Developer application is the second weak point. An overly thick developer coat can mask fine indications, and one that is applied unevenly can leave areas without a proper contrast background. Before we begin we agree with your team how the area will be cleaned, who is responsible for removing coatings, and how long the surface must dry before the examination. That conversation takes only a few minutes at the planning stage and saves a repeat visit.

PT, MT or UT for your Memphis job

Use PT on stainless, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals, or on carbon steel where MT is impractical. Use MT for fast surface checks on carbon and low-alloy steel, and UT when the concern is thickness or an internal flaw. Combined plans are common: PT on a stainless weld, plus UT thickness at adjacent elbows.

faq.q: Can you do dye penetrant inspection on stainless steel in Memphis?
faq.a: Yes. Stainless steel is non-magnetic, so PT is the standard surface method. We use penetrant materials with controlled sulfur, chlorine and fluorine content where the code requires, and we post-clean the part afterward.

faq.q: What kind of defects does liquid penetrant testing find?
faq.a: PT finds discontinuities open to the surface, such as cracks, laps, seams and porosity, on non-porous materials. It cannot find flaws below the surface or covered by smeared metal, plating or coatings.

faq.q: Does temperature affect penetrant testing in Memphis?
faq.a: Yes. The standard method works within a limited temperature range for the part and the materials, and outside it the procedure must be demonstrated at the actual temperature. Summer sun and winter freezes both matter.

faq.q: Is fluorescent penetrant better than visible dye penetrant?
faq.a: Fluorescent penetrant gives the higher sensitivity, yet it must be viewed under UV-A lamps in a dark space. Visible dye penetrant is easier in daylight and in the field, and the code and your service conditions decide which is appropriate.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or team in Memphis?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Memphis. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, so please send the address, access rules and the standard you work under when requesting a quote.

faq.q: Can PT be used on carbon steel?
faq.a: Yes, PT works on carbon steel as well as non-magnetic alloys. Magnetic particle testing is often faster on carbon steel, but PT is used when MT is impractical or when the specification calls for penetrant.

faq.q: What standards cover liquid penetrant examination?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 covers the method for code work, with acceptance in ASME Section VIII Appendix 8, ASME B31.3 or AWS D1.1 depending on the asset. ASTM E165 is the general practice.

faq.q: How should the surface be prepared before PT?
faq.a: Remove paint, scale, oil and weld spatter so crack mouths are open. Avoid peening, shot blasting or wire brushing that could smear metal over cracks; we agree the cleaning method before the examination.

faq.q: Can you train our staff in penetrant testing?
faq.a: Yes. We run PT Level 1 and Level 2 training with a process simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A your company certifies its own people, and we can help you write or review the written practice.
